A figure's *look* is part of its specification, not something applied to it afterwards. Size, type size, spines, panel lettering and colour are all declared, so re-rendering a study on another machine produces the same picture, and changing a journal's column width is one edit rather than a pass over every plotting script.

Two things carry that look. A [`Theme`](../../datamodel/classes/Theme.qmd) is the rule: what each colour *means*, the typeface and its sizes, how heavy a spine is, and how an axis is drawn, meaning who places its ticks, where it ends and whether its spines meet. A study states one, and every figure it lists is drawn by it. The `Figure` owns what is its own, its mosaic and print size, and says where it differs from the rule. Nothing is left to a `.mplstyle` sitting outside the spec where nothing validates it.

## One rule per study

A study names its theme once, usually a fragment under `spec/`:

```yaml
# spec/desc-published_theme.yaml
tvbo_class: tvbo:Theme
ink: "#000000"
font_family: [DejaVu Sans]
font_size: 7
spines: open
ticks: native
axis_ends: data
spine_offset: 0
panel_number_case: lower
```

```yaml
# MyStudy.yaml
theme: !include spec/desc-published_theme.yaml
figures:
  - !include spec/fig-01_desc-overview_figure.yaml
  - !include spec/fig-02_desc-sweep_figure.yaml
```

Every figure in `figures:` is drawn by it, whichever file the figure record came from. A study nested under another takes its parent's theme unless it states its own, so a paper's rule reaches the studies it aggregates without restyling one that reproduces someone else's figures.

The layers, weakest first, each stating only what it changes:

| Layer | Where it is written |
|---|---|
| TVB-O's shipped theme | `tvbo:theme/default`: the colours, and an unboxed legend. It states no axis rule. |
| The house axis rule | `tvbo:theme/bsplot`, taken only by a figure that says `auto_format: true` and only where no theme states a rule. |
| The study's theme | `theme:` on the study. The curated theme it names by `iri` sits underneath its own statements. |
| The figure's theme | `theme:` on the figure, for what this one figure draws differently. |
| The figure's own fields | `font_size`, `dpi`, `spines` and the others in the table below. |

A figure that must be left exactly as its panels drew it says `auto_format: false`: no tick is re-placed, no limit moved, no spine detached or trimmed, whatever the study's theme says.

::: {.callout-important}
A study with no theme follows no axis rule. Its axes carry the backend's own ticks, limits and spines. Earlier versions passed every figure through bsplot's format pass unless it said `auto_format: false`; a study that relied on that states `theme: {iri: tvbo:theme/bsplot}` once and keeps the look.
:::

## What the figure records

These are fields of the `Figure`. The ones marked as overrides are also slots of the theme, where they are the study's default:

| Field | What it fixes |
|---|---|
| `width`, `height` | Physical print size in mm. |
| `dpi` | Raster resolution. Scales pixels only, never the physical size or the type size. Overrides the theme's. |
| `font_size` | Body type size in points, unchanged by `width` or `dpi`. Overrides the theme's, for a figure printed at another width than its siblings. |
| `format` | Output format (`pdf`/`svg`/`png`). Overrides the theme's. |
| `layout`, `height_ratios`, `width_ratios` | The mosaic and the relative size of its rows and columns. |
| `spines`, `spine_offset` | `box` (all four, closed) or `open` (left and bottom), and how far the two scale-bearing ones stand off the plot. Override the theme's. |
| `panel_numbers`, `panel_number_format`, `panel_number_loc`, `panel_number_offset`, `panel_number_size` | Panel lettering: whether, how spelled, which corner, how far in, how large. All but the size override the theme's; the size in points beats the theme's `panel_number_scale`. |
| `trim_margins`, `pad` | Whether the save re-crops to the drawn content, and how much whitespace is left when it does. Override the theme's. |
| `share_x`, `share_y` | Panel groups that end on one scale. |
| `auto_format` | Whether this figure's axes follow a theme's axis rule. `false` leaves them as drawn, `true` asks for the house rule where no theme states one, unset follows the theme. |

Because these are declared, a figure states its print size rather than inheriting one, and nothing else unless it differs from its study:

```yaml
figures:
  - name: Fig2
    layout: "ab/cc"
    width: 180          # mm, a two-column journal figure
    height: 120
  - name: Fig5
    layout: "ab/cd"
    width: 180
    height: 155
    font_size: 13.8     # this one is printed larger than its siblings
    spines: box         # and its heatmaps are framed on four sides
```

::: {.callout-tip}
Set `width` and `font_size` together. Type size is in points and independent of the figure size, so shrinking a figure without raising its `font_size` is what produces the unreadable labels a reviewer will ask about.
:::

## The theme

A theme is one object carrying a project's whole look. Start from a curated one and state only what you change, the same `iri` + merge that an `Observation` or a `Coupling` uses. TVB-O's colours are always the base, so `iri` is only needed to bring in another curated theme, such as the house axis rule:

```yaml
theme:
  iri: tvbo:theme/bsplot
  highlight: "#e4572e"
  tick_length: 3
  axis_width: 0.8
  grid_lines: false
  font_family: [Helvetica, Arial]
```

A slot left unset is not a value: the layer underneath keeps it. So a theme states the look it means to fix and nothing else.

### Colours are named, never written

A theme gives colours *roles*. A panel asks for the role, so recolouring a project is one edit and every figure follows:

| Role | What it is for |
|---|---|
| `ink` | Text, spines and ticks: the near-black everything is read against. |
| `base` | Lines, bars and markers wherever the colour carries no meaning. Leads the cycler. |
| `muted` | Hairlines and de-emphasised strokes: present, and not competing. |
| `highlight` | The single emphasis colour. |
| `background` | The page the figure is printed on. |
| `palette` | The categorical hues, reached into only where a panel separates conditions. |

Two rules make this work. The cycler is `[base] + palette`, so a plot that names no colour comes out in the neutral and only a panel that *means* to separate conditions gets hues. And `highlight` is deliberately outside the cycler, because a colour handed to the second line of every plot cannot also mean *this is the point*.

Anywhere a figure names a colour, a role or a hue is accepted in place of a hex — `Style.color`, a rule's or a region's `color`, and the flat `color` of a surface or network panel:

```yaml
layers:
  - {mark: line, encoding: {x: time, y: rate}, style: {color: highlight}}
rules:
  - {orientation: horizontal, at: [0], color: muted, dash: dashed}
```

Anything that is not a role passes through untouched, so `#0a5170`, `tab:blue` and `red` keep working exactly as before.

::: {.callout-note}
`Encoding.color` is not a colour. `encoding: {x: time, y: rate, color: node}` names the *field* whose values separate the marks, and draws one line per node from the cycler. To fix a mark's colour, use `Style.color`.
:::

### Continuous scales

`colormaps` is an open namespace. `sequential` and `diverging` are always present, because they are the two the renderer reaches for on its own; everything else is a key you name:

```yaml
colormaps:
  sequential: cividis
  bold: viridis
  meg: plasma
  eeg: cividis
```

A layer then names the key (`style: {colormap: meg}`), and anything the theme did not declare falls through to the backend's own registry, so `inferno`, `coolwarm` and `parula` still work. A key that shadows a registered colormap name is refused at load rather than silently redirecting every use of it.

A mark that names no scale is not left to matplotlib's default: it takes `sequential`, or `diverging` when its limits are centred, because a map of signed deviations read on a one-directional ramp is misleading in a way no axis label catches.

```{python}
#| label: fig-roles
#| fig-cap: "The shipped theme: the five roles, then the categorical hues in the order the cycler hands them out."
#| fig-alt: "Two rows of colour swatches. The top row shows ink, base, muted, highlight and background; the bottom row shows the five categorical hues."
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from tvbo.plot import palette

rows = [("roles", [palette.color(r) for r in palette.ROLES], palette.ROLES),
        ("palette", palette.palette(), [f"palette.{i}" for i in range(len(palette.palette()))])]

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(7.5, 2.4))
for ax, (_, colours, labels) in zip(axes, rows):
    for i, (c, label) in enumerate(zip(colours, labels)):
        ax.add_patch(plt.Rectangle((i, 0), 0.92, 1, facecolor=c, edgecolor=palette.muted()))
        ax.text(i + 0.46, -0.18, f"{label}\n{c}", ha="center", va="top", fontsize=7, color=palette.ink())
    ax.set_xlim(-0.1, len(colours)); ax.set_ylim(-0.75, 1.05); ax.set_axis_off()
fig.tight_layout()
```

### The axis rule

How an axis is drawn is four statements, and a theme that makes none of them leaves every axis as the backend drew it.

| Slot | What it decides |
|---|---|
| `ticks` | Who places the ticks of an axis nobody placed ticks on. `native`: the backend's locator, nothing moves. `round`: multiples of a round step, at most `max_ticks` of them. `declared`: only the ticks each panel gives in `xticks`/`yticks`; the render refuses, naming every axis that gives none. |
| `max_ticks`, `tick_steps` | The budget and the multiples that count as round under `round`: 4 ticks and `[1, 2, 5]` unless stated. Adding 2.5 admits 0, 25, 50. |
| `axis_ends` | Where an autoscaled axis ends. `data`: at the data, with the backend's margin. `ticks`: on a tick at both ends, however far the next one lies. `near`: on a tick where one lies within `end_tick_reach` of the data (0.2 of its span unless stated), at the data otherwise. |
| `axis_margin` | How far an axis extends past its data where its end is not on a tick, as a fraction of the span. |
| `spines` | `open` (left and bottom) or `box` (all four). |
| `spine_offset` | How far the left and bottom spines stand off the plot, in axes fractions. 0 makes them meet at the origin. |
| `spine_trim` | End each of those two spines on its outermost ticks instead of running it the length of the axis. |
| `align_labels` | Put the axis labels of neighbouring panels on one line. |
| `colorbar_ends`, `colorbar_outline` | Tick a colour bar at the ends and the centre of its range, each number written in full, instead of on the round values inside it; and whether the bar is framed. |

`axis_ends` exists because an axis cannot always have round ticks, a tick at each end and no empty space at once. Data running from 0.2 to 0.91 gets round ticks at 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8. Ending the axis on a tick at both sides means 0 and 1, and the data then fills 71 % of its panel. Which of the three gives way is a decision about the figure, so the rule states it: `data` gives up the end ticks, `ticks` gives up the space, and `near` takes an end tick only where it is cheap.

What a panel declares always stands. Its `xticks`, `yticks`, `nbins`, limits, a logarithmic scale, the extent of an image and the ticks a custom drawer fixed are never re-placed, whatever the rule says. Panels on a shared scale (`share_x`, `share_y`) are placed from their common extent, so they stay on one scale. A boxed frame ignores `spine_offset` and `spine_trim`, since moving two sides of a closed box opens it.

The rule TVB-O's own figures use is curated as `tvbo:theme/bsplot`: round ticks, `near` ends, spines stood off by 0.02 and trimmed, labels aligned, colour bars ticked at their ends. `tvbo.plot.axis_rule.place(fig, rule)` and `frame(fig, rule)` apply a rule to any matplotlib figure, for plotting code outside a spec.

### The geometry a sheet used to own

| Slot | What it fixes |
|---|---|
| `tick_length`, `tick_width`, `tick_direction`, `tick_pad` | Major tick marks: how long, how heavy, which way, how far from their labels. |
| `minor_ticks`, `minor_tick_length`, `minor_tick_width` | Whether minor ticks are drawn, and their shape. |
| `axis_width` | Weight of the axes frame. A figure whose spines are heavier than its data is drawn the wrong way round. |
| `label_pad`, `title_pad` | Distance from an axis label, and from a panel title, to the axes. |
| `line_width`, `marker_size` | Defaults for any layer whose own style does not fix one. |
| `legend_frame`, `legend_handle_length`, `legend_pad` | The legend box, its sample line, and how far it sits from the axes. TVB-O's own theme is the one place that decides keys are unboxed; a panel overrides it with `legend: {frame: true}`. |
| `grid_lines` | Whether the grid is drawn. Off in most journals, and worth stating either way. Named in full because a panel's `grid:` is the tiling of a `kind: grid`, and one word cannot mean both. |
| `font_family` | Typefaces, most-wanted first. A generic family first (`sans-serif`) selects that family outright. |
| `font_size`, `font_weight` | Body type size in points, and its weight. A figure's own `font_size` beats it. |
| `label_scale`, `tick_label_scale`, `title_scale`, `legend_scale` | The size of axis labels, tick numbers, panel titles and legend text, each as a multiple of the body size. Unset draws it at the body size. |
| `label_weight`, `title_weight`, `title_loc` | Weight of axis labels and panel titles, and where a title sits along the top of its axes. |
| `math_font`, `unicode_minus` | The typeface of mathematical text, and whether a negative number carries a true minus sign. |
| `tick_format`, `exponent_as_power` | `sci` or `plain` numbers on every axis that states no format of its own, and whether a shared exponent reads x10^-3 typeset or 1e-3. |
| `mirror_ticks` | Tick marks on the top and right of a boxed frame as well. |
| `marker_edge_width`, `bar_edge_width`, `line_cap`, `errorbar_cap_size` | Outline weight of markers and of bars, how a line ends, and the caps of an error bar. |
| `legend_loc`, `legend_label_spacing`, `legend_handle_text_pad`, `legend_marker_scale` | Where a legend sits when its panel names no place, and the spacing inside it. |
| `grid_width`, `grid_style`, `grid_below` | Weight and dash of the grid, and whether it runs beneath the data. |
| `panel_numbers`, `panel_number_format`, `panel_number_case`, `panel_number_loc`, `panel_number_offset`, `panel_number_scale`, `panel_number_weight` | Panel letters: whether, how spelled, which case, which corner, how far in, how large against the body size, how heavy. The caption letters each panel in the same case. |
| `dpi`, `format`, `trim_margins`, `pad`, `transparent`, `editable_text` | What is saved: resolution, format, whether the page is cropped to its content or left transparent, and whether text stays text in vector output so a typesetter can edit it. |
| `layout_engine`, `style` | The layout engine that positions the panels, and the style layers underneath the theme. |
| `opts` | Any backend setting no slot names, applied after every slot: `opts: {hatch.linewidth: 0.5}`. |

Every slot is read by the renderer, and a test pins that, so a theme cannot state something that is accepted and then ignored.

### Overriding it per panel

A panel states the same words to override the theme for itself — `tick_length`, `tick_size`, `tick_prune`, `nbins`, `xticks`, `yticks`, `hide_xticklabels`, `hide_yticklabels`, `xtick_rotation`, `ytick_rotation`, `xtick_format`, `ytick_format`, `xtick_side`, `ytick_side`. One vocabulary, so a figure-wide default and a single panel's exception are the same slot at two levels:

```yaml
panels:
  a:
    kind: cartesian
    xticks: [0, 50, 100, 150]
    xtick_rotation: 45
    tick_prune: upper
```

Three of them have no theme-wide twin on purpose. `tick_size` would fight the declared type sizes, and `nbins` and `tick_prune` answer to one panel's neighbours, where a corner tick collides or how dense a cell is, rather than to the project's look. A panel that states `nbins` keeps the backend's locator on that budget; the theme's `max_ticks` is the budget of its own `round` rule.

Reference lines, shaded regions and the 3-D viewpoint are declared here too, each carrying the colour that has to travel with it:

```yaml
    rules:
      - {orientation: diagonal, at: [1, 0], color: muted, dash: dashed}   # the identity line
      - {orientation: horizontal, at: [0], color: muted}
    regions:
      - {bounds: [0.2, 0.6, -0.1, 0.4], color: highlight, fill: true, opacity: 0.12}
    camera: {elevation: 22, azimuth: -60}
```

So is the rest of the panel's frame — its labels, limits, scales and shape — which the [figure spec page](index.qmd#what-a-panels-axes-say) lays out in full. Nothing about how an axis is drawn is an option any more: a spec written against the older flat spelling (`axvline` beside `axvline_color`, `elev` beside `azim`, a `legend` that meant a boolean in one panel and a corner in the next) is refused with the replacement named, and `python scripts/migrate_panel_marks.py <tree>` converts a study and reports anything it cannot convert safely.

## Style layers

`style`, on a theme or on a figure, is what sits underneath the theme, and it is for looks TVB-O does not own: bsplot's registered styles, a journal's sheet, the rcParams of a paper being reproduced.

| Written as | What it contributes |
|---|---|
| `tvbo`, `nature` | A registered bsplot style: the house look in one word. |
| `style/study.mplstyle` | A study's own matplotlib defaults, for anything the spec has no field for. |
| `tvbo-palette` | An alias for `theme: {iri: tvbo:theme/default}`, kept because it reads well in a list. |

**Whatever the theme states beats every layer, always.** That is the whole point of separating them: a figure's look can be read off its own spec instead of reconstructed from the sheets underneath it, and a sheet cannot quietly reintroduce a colour cycle the project has replaced.

A palette YAML is no longer a style layer. Naming one raises, and says to declare it as the theme instead.

Reaching for a sheet is deliberate. `style: [tvbo]` is the default when nothing is declared, and a replication that must reproduce a paper's own colours declares its own sheet and *does not* add a theme that would overwrite them.

## Your own theme

A theme is an ordinary TVB-O document. A study keeps it under `spec/`, named with the `_theme` suffix, and includes it once:

```yaml
# spec/desc-house_theme.yaml
tvbo_class: tvbo:Theme
base: "#333333"
highlight: "#e4572e"
palette: ["#2e86ab", "#a23b72", "#f18f01"]
tick_length: 3
grid_lines: false
```

```yaml
theme: !include spec/desc-house_theme.yaml
```

Because it declares its class, `tvbo validate schema spec/desc-house_theme.yaml` checks it like any other document, `tvbo validate study` checks its name against its class, and a misspelt slot is refused rather than silently ignored. A figure that differs states only the difference:

```yaml
figures:
  - {name: Fig2}
  - {name: Fig3}
  - {name: FigS1, theme: {grid_lines: true, font_family: [DejaVu Sans]}}
```

A colormap key takes either a registered name or the colours to ramp between:

```yaml
colormaps:
  sequential: ["#0b1d26", "#1f7d78", "#f2f5f4"]
```

## From your own plotting code

A [custom panel](custom-panels.qmd) draws with matplotlib directly, so it reads the palette rather than the spec:

```{python}
#| label: palette-api
#| code-fold: false
from tvbo.plot import palette

print("roles     ", palette.ink(), palette.base(), palette.muted(), palette.highlight())
print("one hue   ", palette.color("palette.1"))     # counting from zero
print("first three", palette.palette(3))
print("cycler    ", palette.cycle())                # [base] + palette
print("diverging ", palette.colormap("diverging").name)
print("ordinal   ", len(palette.ramp(4)), "steps sampled across the sequential scale")
```

`palette.ramp(n)` is what an *ordered* set of classes should use. A ladder of rungs or a set of ordered bins is not categorical, and drawing it in `palette()` hues tells the reader the classes are unrelated when the whole point is that they are not.

To make a palette current inside a script, hand `use()` a path or a mapping:

```python
palette.use("style/my_palette.yaml")
```

That also writes the colours into the matplotlib rcParams that carry them, so `text.color`, `image.cmap`, the facecolors and the cycler all follow, and code that names no colour at all still comes out in the project's.

## What a sheet still owns

Very little. The theme has a slot for what real study sheets set, and `opts` takes any backend setting it has no slot for, so a study rarely needs a sheet of its own. What a sheet remains good for is a look that already exists as one, a journal's or a published repository's: name it in `style:`, and the theme still wins over it on everything it states.
